item.title: Welcome to the new SAA website
item.dc:creator: SAA Executive Committee
item.description:
We are relaunching the website of the Sequence Analysis Association. The new site is built with Quarto and is open to everyone — there is no longer a member area, and all content, from the webinar programme to the annual reports, is available to all visitors.

What’s new:

  • A new logo and visual identity: the signet is a small sequence index plot, and colours and fonts are defined once in a brand.yml file that can be reused for slides, reports and other formats.
  • A simpler structure: About, Events, Resources and this blog.
  • An RSS feed so you can follow SAA news in your favourite reader.

Feedback is very welcome at info@sequenceanalysis.org.

item.title: ggseqplot 1.0.0 on CRAN
item.dc:creator: Marcel Raab
item.description:
For several years now, Emanuela Struffolino and I have been teaching “Sequence Analysis” in the amazing GESIS Workshops program. Before each course, we send the participants instructions on which software to install in advance. One part of this setup is GraphViz, which TraMineR::seqtreedisplay requires to render tree-structured plots. Quite regularly, installing GraphViz, and sometimes also getting it to work with R, causes some hiccups. For this reason, I had long planned to add a GraphViz-free function for this type of plot to {ggseqplot}. However, the package is just a small side project, and I am not a very skilled programmer. So this plot type, like a few others I wanted to add, never made it into the package. Over the years, the package was maintained but not really improved. AI tools, on the other hand, have improved quite dramatically during the same time.

Nudged by this year’s iteration of our course, I therefore decided to use Claude Code to help me implement the missing plot functions. This was the first time I used AI tools to work on the package, and I have to admit it was a very pleasant experience. I am pretty sure that without this powerful tool, I would not have added these long-missing functions to the package.

Version 1.0.0 of {ggseqplot} is now on CRAN and adds three new plot types:

  • ggseqtreeplot() renders regression trees of sequences (TraMineR::seqtree) — without requiring GraphViz, which TraMineR::seqtreedisplay needs.
  • ggseqpcplot() draws decorated parallel coordinate plots, reproducing TraMineR::seqpcplot.
  • ggseqimplicplot() plots the implicative statistic computed with TraMineRextras::seqimplic.

This post briefly shows the three functions and how their appearance can be adjusted. See the NEWS file for all changes.

Example data

We use a sample of 300 school-to-work trajectories from the well-known mvad data in {TraMineR}.

library(TraMineR)
library(ggseqplot)
library(ggplot2)

data(mvad)
set.seed(1)
mvad <- mvad[sample(nrow(mvad), 300), ]

## State properties: alphabet, short and long labels,
## ordered from education via training to the labor market
mvad.alphabet <- c("school", "FE", "HE", "training", "employment", "joblessness")
mvad.lab <- c("school", "further education", "higher education",
              "training", "employment", "joblessness")
mvad.shortlab <- c("SC", "FE", "HE", "TR", "EM", "JL")

mvad.seq <- seqdef(mvad[, 17:86], alphabet = mvad.alphabet,
                   states = mvad.shortlab, labels = mvad.lab, xtstep = 6)

Regression tree plots

First, we grow a regression tree of the sequences with TraMineR::seqtree, using Hamming distances and four covariates.

mvad.diss <- seqdist(mvad.seq, method = "HAM")
mvad.tree <- seqtree(mvad.seq ~ male + Grammar + funemp + gcse5eq,
                     data = mvad, diss = mvad.diss, R = 100, max.depth = 3)

Default output

By default, every node of the tree shows a state distribution plot (type = "d"), and the legend and the global quality measures of the tree are placed below the tree.

ggseqtreeplot(mvad.tree)

Other node plots are available via type, e.g. index plots ("i"), sequence frequency plots ("f"), modal state plots ("ms") or mean time plots ("mt").

Adjusting the node plots

The node plots are drawn as images onto the tree. Hence, they cannot be changed afterwards with +. Instead, scales, themes and other ggplot components for all node plots are passed to the node.layers argument. The tree as a whole — legend, title, quality measures — can be adjusted with the usual {ggplot2} functions.

The following plot comes closer to the look of TraMineR::seqtreedisplay: the node plots have no axis labels, the legend is placed in the upper left corner, and the goodness-of-fit measures (printed in separate lines with quality.multiline = TRUE) in the upper right corner. Since the axis labels are removed, plot.margin is required to even out the space around the node plots.

ggseqtreeplot(mvad.tree, quality.multiline = TRUE,
              node.layers = theme(axis.text = element_blank(),
                                  axis.ticks = element_blank(),
                                  axis.line = element_blank(),
                                  plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 4, 6))) +
  theme(# global quality measures (rendered as plot tag) in the upper right corner
        plot.tag.location = "panel",
        plot.tag.position = c(1, 1),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 1, vjust = 1),
        # legend in the upper left corner, one entry per line
        legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0, 1),
        legend.justification = c(0, 1),
        legend.direction = "vertical")

For large trees, I recommend saving the plot with a generous size, e.g. ggsave("tree.png", width = 14, height = 9).

Decorated parallel coordinate plots

Decorated parallel coordinate plots (Bürgin & Ritschard, 2014, doi:10.1080/00031305.2014.887591) draw each distinct sequence as a line connecting its successive states. The size of the squares and the width of the lines are proportional to the (weighted) number of sequences following a pattern. As in the TraMineR::seqpcplot examples, we use the first 20 weighted family-life sequences of the biofam data (ages 15 to 30; sum of weights = 18).

data(biofam)
lab <- c("Parent", "Left", "Married", "Left+Marr", "Child", "Left+Child",
         "Left+Marr+Child", "Divorced")
biofam.seq <- seqdef(data = biofam[, 10:25], labels = lab,
                     weights = biofam$wp00tbgs)
biofam.seq <- biofam.seq[1:20, ]

Default output

With order.align = "time", the x-axis shows the sequence position at which a state is observed. In the example, the position corresponds to the respondent’s age.

ggseqpcplot(biofam.seq, order.align = "time")

Distinct successive states and highlighted patterns

All arguments of TraMineR::seqpcplot that affect the computation can be passed on via .... Below, order.align = "first" aligns the distinct successive states (DSS) instead of time, group produces one plot per sex, and the filter argument colors only the most frequent patterns that together cover 50% of the sequences, while the remaining ones are grayed out. Titles and labels are changed with the usual {ggplot2} functions.

ggseqpcplot(biofam.seq, order.align = "first", group = biofam$sex[1:20],
            filter = list(type = "function", value = "cumfreq", level = 0.5),
            seed = 2, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Family-life trajectories by sex",
       subtitle = "colored: most frequent patterns covering 50% of the (weighted) sequences",
       x = "Order of distinct successive states") +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

Implicative statistic

The implicative statistic (TraMineRextras::seqimplic) shows how strongly membership in a group implies being in a certain state at a given position. Here we compare young people with and without five or more GCSE passes at grade C or higher (gcse5eq) using the mvad.seq defined above.

Default output

ggseqimplicplot(mvad.seq, group = mvad$gcse5eq)

Values above the dotted reference line indicate that the implication is significant at the 95% level.

Design adjustments

Because the result is a regular ggplot, its appearance can be changed with common {ggplot2} commands. In the example, we specify yearly axis labels, add more informative facet titles, apply the colorblind-friendly Okabe-Ito palette (via {paletteer}), request a one-row legend with thicker keys, and use a larger base font size (theme_minimal() is already the default theme of the function).

library(paletteer)

ggseqimplicplot(mvad.seq, group = mvad$gcse5eq, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 70, by = 12), labels = 1993:1998,
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
  scale_color_paletteer_d("colorblindr::OkabeIto") +
  # legend in one row; thicker lines in the legend keys
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1, override.aes = list(linewidth = 4))) +
  facet_wrap(~group, labeller = as_labeller(c(no = "Fewer than 5 GCSEs",
                                              yes = "5 or more GCSEs"))) +
  labs(title = "Which states are implied by school performance?",
       x = NULL, y = "Implicative statistic", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 12),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

Further information

  • {ggseqplot} website with reference pages and a vignette (which does not yet cover the new functions)
  • Issues and feature requests: https://github.com/maraab23/ggseqplot/issues

item.title: Validating sequence analysis typologies using parametric bootstrap
item.dc:creator: Matthias Studer
item.description:
This tutorial was first published on the old SAA website in October 2023. It has been re-run in October 2026 with {TraMineR} 2.2.14 and {WeightedCluster} 2.0. Because the bootstrap relies on random draws, the bootstrapped values may differ slightly from the original post.

Introduction

This document provides a very quick introduction to the R code needed to use parametric bootstraps for typology validation in sequence analysis. Readers interested in the methods and the exact interpretation of the results are referred to:

  • Studer, M. (2021). Validating sequence analysis typologies using parametric bootstraps. Sociological Methodology, 51(2), 290–318. https://doi.org/10.1177/00811750211014232

Creating the state sequence object

For this example, we will use the mvad dataset. Let’s start with the creation of the state sequence object.

## Loading the TraMineR library
library(TraMineR)
## Loading the data
data(mvad)

## State properties
mvad.alphabet <- c(
  "employment",
  "FE",
  "HE",
  "joblessness",
  "school",
  "training"
)
mvad.lab <- c(
  "employment",
  "further education",
  "higher education",
  "joblessness",
  "school",
  "training"
)
mvad.shortlab <- c("EM", "FE", "HE", "JL", "SC", "TR")

## Creating the state sequence object
mvad.seq <- seqdef(
  mvad,
  17:86,
  alphabet = mvad.alphabet,
  states = mvad.shortlab,
  labels = mvad.lab,
  xtstep = 6
)

Creating the typology

We will now create a typology using cluster analysis. Readers interested in more detail are referred to the WeightedCluster library manual, which goes into the details of the creation and computation of cluster quality measures.

We start by computing dissimilarities with the seqdist function and the Hamming distance. We then use Ward clustering to create a typology of the trajectories. For this step, we recommend the use of the fastcluster library, which considerably speeds up the computations.

## Using fastcluster for hierarchical clustering
library(fastcluster)
## Distance computation
diss <- seqdist(mvad.seq, method = "HAM")
## Hierarchical clustering
hc <- hclust(as.dist(diss), method = "ward.D")

We can now compute several cluster quality indices using the as.clustrange function from two to ten groups.

# Loading the WeightedCluster library
library(WeightedCluster)
# Computing cluster quality measures.
clustqual <- as.clustrange(hc, diss = diss, ncluster = 10)
clustqual
           PBC   HG HGSD  ASW ASWw     CH   R2   CHsq R2sq   HC
cluster2  0.55 0.71 0.69 0.39 0.39 184.57 0.21 347.47 0.33 0.14
cluster3  0.49 0.57 0.57 0.27 0.27 139.53 0.28 261.70 0.42 0.22
cluster4  0.46 0.58 0.57 0.24 0.24 124.40 0.35 228.94 0.49 0.23
cluster5  0.51 0.68 0.67 0.27 0.28 118.20 0.40 241.78 0.58 0.18
cluster6  0.52 0.70 0.70 0.28 0.29 117.08 0.45 241.96 0.63 0.17
cluster7  0.55 0.78 0.78 0.32 0.32 114.14 0.49 245.83 0.68 0.13
cluster8  0.56 0.82 0.82 0.32 0.33 109.22 0.52 244.85 0.71 0.11
cluster9  0.57 0.85 0.85 0.34 0.35 105.74 0.55 255.12 0.74 0.09
cluster10 0.55 0.85 0.84 0.32 0.33 101.81 0.57 244.05 0.76 0.10

Parametric bootstrap

Parametric bootstrap aims to provide baseline values obtained by clustering similar but non-clustered data. This can be computed using the seqnullcqi function with the following parameters:

  • R: number of bootstraps.
  • model: the null model (see the sections below).
  • seqdist.args: list of arguments passed to seqdist (should be identical to the first call to seqdist).
  • hclust.method: hierarchical clustering method (should be identical to the original clustering).
  • kmedoid: if TRUE, use PAM (and the wcKMedRange function) instead of hierarchical clustering.
  • parallel: if TRUE, use parallel computing to speed up the computations.

Combined randomization

The following R code estimates expected values of the cluster quality indices when clustering similar sequences that are not clustered according to the "combined" model, using the Hamming distance and Ward hierarchical clustering. We set parallel = TRUE to use parallel computing. You can use progressbar = TRUE to show a progress bar of the computations (not meaningful here within a document).

set.seed(1)
bcq.combined <- seqnullcqi(
  mvad.seq,
  clustqual,
  R = 1000,
  model = "combined",
  seqdist.args = list(method = "HAM"),
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  parallel = TRUE
)

Once the parametric bootstrap is computed (may take a while…), the results are stored in the bcq.combined object. Printing the object (just by writing its name) already provides several pieces of information: the standardized cluster quality indices and the inconclusive interval (standardized values).

Several plots can then be used to inspect the results using the plot command and the type argument. First, one can look at the sequences generated by the null model by using type = "seqdplot".

plot(bcq.combined, type = "seqdplot")

The overall distribution of the CQI values can be plotted using type = "density". In this case, one also needs to specify the CQI to be used. All tested numbers of groups are found to be significant. Any CQI computed by as.clustrange() can be used here. To show the density of the average silhouette width ("ASW"), one can use:

plot(bcq.combined, stat = "ASW", type = "density")
      2.5%      97.5% 
-0.2176533  2.3174904

By using type = "line", we plot the obtained and bootstrapped CQI values depending on the number of groups.

plot(bcq.combined, stat = "ASW", type = "line")

Randomized sequencing

To use another null model, one only needs to change the model argument of the seqnullcqi function. The randomized sequencing keeps the duration attached to each state, but randomizes the ordering of the spells. It can be used to uncover the sequencing structure of the data.

set.seed(2)
bcq.seq <- seqnullcqi(
  mvad.seq,
  clustqual,
  R = 1000,
  model = "sequencing",
  seqdist.args = list(method = "HAM"),
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  parallel = TRUE
)

We can then plot the results as before. Notice that solutions between 3 and 6 are below the critical line.

plot(bcq.seq, stat = "ASW", type = "line")

Randomized duration

The randomized duration keeps the same ordering of the states, but randomizes the time spent in each spell. It can be used to uncover the duration-related structure of the data.

set.seed(3)
bcq.dur <- seqnullcqi(
  mvad.seq,
  clustqual,
  R = 1000,
  model = "duration",
  seqdist.args = list(method = "HAM"),
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  parallel = TRUE
)

We can then plot the results as before. The 3- and 4-group solutions are below the “significance line”. Otherwise, the ranking of the solutions is the same.

plot(bcq.dur, stat = "ASW", type = "line")

State independence

The state independence null model generates sequences, position by position, independently of the previous state. This is a quite unrealistic assumption for longitudinal data.

set.seed(4)
bcq.stateindep <- seqnullcqi(
  mvad.seq,
  clustqual,
  R = 1000,
  model = "stateindep",
  seqdist.args = list(method = "HAM"),
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  parallel = TRUE
)

Bootstrapped CQI values are extremely low compared to our clustering, meaning that we have a strong longitudinal structure (not surprising!).

plot(bcq.stateindep, stat = "ASW", type = "line")

First-order Markov null model

The first-order Markov null model generates sequences using time-invariant transition rates. As a result, the generated sequences are often quite similar to the observed ones. This model can uncover structure stemming from time-dependent transition rates.

set.seed(5)
bcq.Markov <- seqnullcqi(
  mvad.seq,
  clustqual,
  R = 1000,
  model = "Markov",
  seqdist.args = list(method = "HAM"),
  hclust.method = "ward.D",
  parallel = TRUE
)
plot(bcq.Markov, stat = "ASW", type = "line")

Choosing a solution

The various null models lead to the same conclusions and ranking of the solutions. Solutions between 3 and 6 groups were not always above the critical lines (in the sequencing null model for instance), and can be avoided. We generally saw good clustering quality for a clustering in 9 groups. The solution is shown below.

seqdplot(mvad.seq, clustqual$clustering$cluster9, border = NA)

item.title: ggseqplot: ggplotify sequence plots
item.dc:creator: Marcel Raab
item.description:
This guest post was first published on the old SAA website in August 2022. It has been re-rendered in October 2026 with {ggseqplot} 1.0.0 and {TraMineR} 2.2.14.

Intro

We all know that visualization plays an important role when conducting a sequence analysis. Accordingly, {TraMineR} and other sequence analysis libraries provide a rich set of plotting functions. Although the default output of these functions often is almost publication-ready, it is usually necessary to adjust some parameters of the plots to obtain the desired results. In the case of TraMineR::seqplot this requires engaging with base R’s plot environment. Today, however, many R users prefer {ggplot2} over base R’s plot library to produce their visualization and aren’t familiar with plot.

In view of that, I wrote the little R library {ggseqplot} that uses {ggplot2} to render sequence plots. The package complements the standard {TraMineR} workflow, assuming that you are defining and analyzing your sequence data using {TraMineR} functions. Only the visualization is outsourced to {ggseqplot}. Accordingly, {ggseqplot} functions are structured in a similar fashion as their {TraMineR} counterparts, often using identical function arguments and also relying on sequence data defined by TraMineR::seqdef as starting point. Under the hood, {ggseqplot} functions are reshaping the data into the format required by {ggplot2} and then call {ggplot2} functions to render the plots.

Apart from a few layout choices, the resulting plots are quite similar to those produced by TraMineR::seqplot. The key difference, however, is that the appearance of those plots can be easily changed by using the + operator and other {ggplot2} functions.

Example set up

# required libraries
library(TraMineR)
library(ggseqplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)
library(ggh4x)
library(patchwork)

## The well-known example data from the TraMineR documentation
data(actcal)
set.seed(1)
actcal <- actcal[sample(nrow(actcal), 300), ]
actcal.lab <- c("> 37 hours", "19-36 hours", "1-18 hours", "no work")
actcal.seq <- seqdef(actcal, 13:24, labels = actcal.lab)

Standard index plot

Example 1

# TraMineR
seqIplot(actcal.seq, sortv = "from.end")
# ggseqplot
ggseqiplot(actcal.seq, sortv = "from.end")

More index plots: utilizing ggplot2 capabilities

Example 2

In the following example, we illustrate how the plot’s appearance can be dramatically changed using standard {ggplot2} functions and two functions from the {colorspace} library (scale_fill_discrete_sequential and scale_color_discrete_sequential). We use these functions to change the color palette and the overall orientation of the index plot. Following the example of many of Raffaella Piccarreta’s sequence visualizations, the following index plot maps the time dimension on the y-axis.

ggseqiplot(actcal.seq, sortv = "from.end") +
  # Use Built-in Constant (months abbreviations) for axis labels
  scale_x_discrete(labels = month.abb) +
  # change the color palette (fill and border color)
  scale_fill_discrete_sequential("heat") +
  scale_color_discrete_sequential("heat") +
  # add a title and a axis title
  labs(x = "Month", title = "Piccarreta-flavored Index Plot") +
  # let the time run "bottom-up" instead of "left-right"
  coord_flip() +
  # Change the position and size of the title and the legend position
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 22),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )

Example 3

The following plots illustrate three options for rendering grouped index plots. The first plot resembles the default output of TraMineR::seqIplot. This type of plot might be misleading if it’s not interpreted carefully because it somewhat hides the group size differences. The same amount of ink is devoted to each of the groups.

The second plot takes care of this, by fixing the y-axis. The group size differences are fully revealed, but there is also a lot of white space.

The third approach is more parsimonious in the sense that there is less empty space in the plot. By using ggh4x::force_panelsizes the height of the index plots is adjusted to their relative group size.

# generate a group vector
set.seed(030583)
grp <- sample(1:3, 300, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.2, .5, .3))

# Variations of grouped index plots

# baseline plot
ggseqiplot(actcal.seq, group = grp)
# internal argument to fix the axis
ggseqiplot(actcal.seq, group = grp, facet_scale = "fixed")
# using ggh4x to get varying plot sizes

# a vector storing the heights of the subplots
rowheight <- table(grp) / 300

ggseqiplot(actcal.seq, group = grp, facet_ncol = 1) +
  force_panelsizes(rows = rowheight) +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))

Additional features

Example 4

Following a suggestion of Claus Wilke, ggseqdplot provides a feature that eases the comparison of state distributions by disaggregating the standard stacked distribution plot.

ggseqdplot(actcal.seq, group = actcal$sex)
ggseqdplot(actcal.seq, group = actcal$sex, dissect = "row")

Example 5

In addition to the sequence plots of TraMineR::seqplot and TraMineRextras::seqplot.rf, I added one additional function for plotting transition rate matrices of sequence states.

By default, the function is visualizing a DSS formatted version of the sequence data. Below, we compare the transition matrices of the same sequence data, first using the STS format and then the DSS format.

p.sts <- ggseqtrplot(actcal.seq, dss = FALSE) +
  ggtitle("STS format")
p.dss <- ggseqtrplot(actcal.seq) +
  ggtitle("DSS format")

# show side by side using patchwork library
p.sts + p.dss & theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 18))

📣 {ggseqplot} website

item.title: TraMineR and TraMineRextras updates 2020–2021
item.dc:creator: SAA Executive Committee
item.description:
This post brings together three release notes on TraMineR and TraMineRextras that appeared on the old SAA website between April 2020 and June 2021. For later changes, see the NEWS files of the packages on CRAN.

TraMineR 2.2-2 (3 June 2021)

  • All new indexes proposed in Ritschard, G. Measuring the nature of individual sequences. Sociological Methods & Research. DOI: 10.1177/00491241211036156 — see function seqindic().
  • Function dissdomassoc(), which computes the measures of association between domains proposed in Piccarreta, R. (2017). Joint sequence analysis: Association and clustering. Sociological Methods & Research, 46(2), 252–287. DOI: 10.1177/0049124115591013.
  • Updated seqdist(), which can now compute pairwise dissimilarities between two (sub)sets of state sequences.

TraMineRextras 0.6.1 (January 2021)

  • Dynamic individual indicators following Pelletier, D., Bignami-Van Assche, S. & Simard-Gendron, A. (2020). Measuring life course complexity with dynamic sequence analysis. Social Indicators Research. DOI: 10.1007/s11205-020-02464-y
  • Polyadic distances and their comparison with distances computed on randomly drawn polyads, as described in Liao, T. F. (2021). Using sequence analysis to quantify how strongly life courses are linked. Sociological Science, 8, 48–72. DOI: 10.15195/v8.a3

TraMineR 2.2 and TraMineRextras 0.6 (April 2020)

TraMineR 2.2 improved the seqdist() function:

  • vectors of state-dependent indel costs are supported by all distance methods that require an indel value;
  • indel has a new default "auto", which derives a suitable indel value from the substitution costs;
  • refseq (reference sequence) is supported by all distance methods, including a reference given as a sequence object;
  • normalization is available for all edit distances.

In addition, seqdef() assigns a default colour palette for alphabets with more than 12 states, and a new rbind() method for state sequence objects makes it easy to merge sequence data.

TraMineRextras 0.6 added seqCompare(), which implements the likelihood ratio test (LRT) and the BIC difference proposed in Liao, T. F. & Fasang, A. E. (2021). Comparing groups of life-course sequences using the Bayesian information criterion and the likelihood-ratio test. Sociological Methodology, 51(1), 44–85. DOI: 10.1177/0081175020959401. Moreover, seqplot.rf() gained the argument which.plot, and seqgranularity() the methods "first.valid" and "last.valid" for sequences with missing values.

item.title: New R package: seqhandbook
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Robette
item.description:
Hello everyone, I just uploaded a new R package on CRAN, seqhandbook. It is initially intended to accompany a sequence analysis handbook to be published (in French) in 2021 by INED, with some data sets and a tutorial.

But it also includes functions for

  • describing episodes in individual sequences,
  • measuring association between domains in multidimensional sequence analysis,
  • heat maps of sequence data,
  • Globally Interdependent Multidimensional Sequence Analysis (GIMSA),
  • smoothing sequences for index plots,
  • coding sequences for Qualitative Harmonic Analysis,
  • measuring stress from multidimensional scaling factors, and
  • symmetrical (or canonical) Partial Least Squares.

Maybe some of them could be useful for you!

Best,
Nicolas
